picked.t: Vietnam proposes workday swap to create 4-day weekend for Culture Day holiday in November
picked.body: After consulting with 13 government agencies, ministries, and sectors, the ministry recommended that civil servants and public employees swap their Monday, Nov. 23 workday for Saturday, Nov. 28. This adjustment, pending the Prime Minister's approval would create an uninterrupted break from Saturday, Nov. 21 through Tuesday, Nov. 24. The extended holiday period consists of the standard weekend, the swapped day off, and the official Culture Day on Tuesday. This marks the first year workers will receive full pay for this newly established holiday. The ministry emphasized that a continuous four-day break will give citizens ample time to engage in family, community, and local events. Officials believe this will improve public access to the arts while simultaneously boosting the cultural, tourism, and service industries. The Politburo, the top decision-making body of the Communist Party of Vietnam, selected Nov. 24 to commemorate the first National Cultural Conference in 1946, which was chaired by President Ho Chi Minh. By designating this date as a public holiday, the government aims to encourage creativity, foster a civilized lifestyle, and give the public more opportunities to enjoy national heritage. The legislative National Assembly officially approved the paid day off during its April session. In early September, the government moved to codify this provision into the Labor Code. The bill is expected to pass during the National Assembly's October session. In addition to the Culture Day proposal, the Ministry of Home Affairs also submitted its recommended schedule for the 2027 Lunar New Year ( Tet ) holiday. This proposed break would span seven days, beginning on Feb. 4, 2027, and concluding on Feb. 10, 2027. Under this plan, civil servants and public employees would return to work on Feb. 11. Furthermore, the 2027 National Day holiday is slated to be a four-day weekend from Sept. 2 through Sept. 5, combining the two official public holidays with the standard weekend. With the recent addition of Culture Day, Vietnam's 12 annual paid public holidays now include: New Year's Day (one day), Lunar New Year (five days), Hung Kings' Commemoration Day (one day), Reunification Day on April 30 (one day), Labor Day on May 1 (one day), National Day (two days), and Vietnamese Culture Day (one day).

picked.t: Canadian seafood imports surge 40% as lobster, snow crab gain favor in Vietnam
picked.body: The country imported $61 million worth of Canadian seafood in 2025, up from $49 million in 2024 and $44 million in 2023, according to Vietnam Customs. The upward trend has continued this year, with imports reaching $43.2 million in the first eight months, a 28.2% increase from the same period last year. The growth comes as seafood businesses in Nova Scotia, Canada’s leading seafood-exporting province, look to expand into new markets. Lobster is the province’s flagship seafood product, accounting for more than half of its total export value in 2025. With exports of live lobster down 19%, Nova Scotia is increasingly seeking opportunities in markets including Vietnam. Canadian snow crab and lobster are now widely available at seafood retailers across Vietnam. A manager at a seafood shop on Ly Tu Trong Street in Ho Chi Minh City’s Ben Thanh Ward said consumers are attracted to Canadian products because of their relatively competitive prices and consistent quality. Canadian lobsters weighing 500–600 grams sell for around VND950,000–1.1 million (US$37–38) per kilogram, while those weighing at least one kilogram cost about VND1.3–1.4 million. That is considerably cheaper than Australian lobster, priced at around VND3.5 million per kilogram, and domestic green lobster, which sells for about VND1.5 million. Live Canadian snow crab is priced at around VND1.4–1.5 million per kilogram, roughly 30% less than some other imported crab varieties. Canadian oysters cost more than VND400,000 per kilogram, compared with as much as VND1 million for certain French varieties. Tran Van Truong, CEO of seafood chain Hai San Hoang Gia, said stable and competitive pricing has helped make Canadian seafood affordable to a broader range of consumers. Preferential tariffs have also helped keep prices down. Canadian lobsters that meet the requirements of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership are subject to a 0% import tariff in Vietnam. Jason Hollett, Nova Scotia’s deputy minister of agriculture and deputy minister of fisheries and aquaculture, said Vietnam is currently the province’s seventh-largest seafood export market. He made the remarks while leading a delegation of Canadian seafood businesses to Vietnam in September to meet local companies and explore business opportunities. Provincial authorities said Nova Scotia’s premium seafood products account for 29% of Canada’s total seafood export value worldwide. Snow crab is Nova Scotia’s largest seafood export to Vietnam by volume, with exports valued at around CAD35 million (US$25.3 million) in 2025, while lobster exports were worth about CAD8 million (US$5.8 million).

picked.t: Woman abandons city career to turn 6 hectares of family forest into $380,000-a-year business
picked.body: Trang, 44, began building Ca Mau Eco a little over three years ago on just over six hectares of family land in Da Bac Commune, Ca Mau, which is Vietnam's southernmost province. The plot holds melaleuca forest and open water, and sits on the road to Da Bac and Song Doc. It runs up against U Minh Ha National Park, one of three core zones of the Mui Ca Mau World Biosphere Reserve that UNESCO recognized in 2009. She left most of the land under melaleuca, set the buildings into the existing landscape and kept concrete to a minimum. Visitors paddle sampans, fish, make folk cakes and wear ao ba ba , the traditional southern blouse, for activities in the water. They also hear the tall tales of Bac Ba Phi, the U Minh farmer whose deadpan stories about the forest's abundance became southern folklore. There are performances on the river and don ca tai tu , the southern chamber music UNESCO added to its intangible heritage list in 2013. "I want visitors who come here to have more than a place to enjoy themselves, to be able to feel the space, the way of life and the cultural traits tied to this river country," she said. Da Bac is her mother's home village. Trang graduated in business administration in 2007 and stayed in Ho Chi Minh City to work in the field. In 2012 she quit her job as head of administration and human resources at a large company. She wanted a child, and she wanted to raise that child near family in a calmer place than the city. Back in Ca Mau, she built rental rooms and borrowed from a bank to farm crocodiles. She studied the techniques closely and traveled abroad to learn the trade. The breeding stock however ran into problems and crocodile prices fell, and the operation lost money steadily. At one point the animals died en masse, a loss she puts at around VND1 billion ($38,000). She gave up on crocodiles and went back to the rental rooms and to raising her child. Unaccustomed to sitting still, she later spent about two years at a garment company in Ca Mau. She later resigned as the workload grew and she found herself missing her child's preschool years. She still wanted a business that could draw on what her home region already had. While caring for her child, she began thinking seriously about the family's six hectares. Her first plan was to lease the land, with preference for anyone who wanted to run tourism on it. Showing the plot one day, she met a prospective tenant with the same idea, and the two began discussing a partnership. Her savings and further bank loans went into the project, more than VND10 billion by her account. With no experience in tourism, she learned as she built. She worked out how to lay out and construct each component, and enrolled in a cooking course to prepare for feeding guests. She handled much of the detail herself, from the sampans and thatched huts down to the planting. A full-service design firm would have cost more than she wanted to spend and come with ideas she did not want, so she built piece by piece and kept the concept hers. Her partner pulled his money out while the site was still being finished. Most of her capital was already in the ground with much of the work incomplete, and she drew on family funds to keep going. About six months in, with the site roughly 80% complete, she opened to visitors and kept building around them. Early guests responded well, she says, and she put more money in. She has since worked with tour operators and neighbors to build experiences tied to local life, including harvesting wild honey, checking fish traps, foraging and walking the melaleuca forest. Ca Mau Eco charges no admission and no parking fee, and does not require visitors to buy meals. "I want to create a tourism site that families without much money can still come to on a weekend," she said. Deciding the history of U Minh Ha mattered as much as its scenery, she later built a forest village about 200 m long. It is a run of thatched huts and set pieces recreating life in the forest during the war. The model draws on the Vo Doi forest village inside the national park nearby, one of a network of settlements built into the melaleuca between 1958 and 1960. Camouflaged stilt houses there served as homes, storehouses, a clinic, a school and weapons and food depots. The Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism ranked the Vo Doi site a national historical relic on June 20, 2018. To keep her version close to the record, she went through local historical material, sat with veteran revolutionaries, consulted specialists and talked to people who had lived at Vo Doi. She chose the details so that younger visitors could picture how people ate, worked and held on under the canopy. Three years in, Trang says the site draws several thousand visitors a month, two to three times that over holidays. picked.t: Vietnam may take 7 days off for Lunar New Year in early 2027
picked.body: The ministry filed the plan on Sept. 11, Nguyen Thi Quyen, deputy director of its Department of Employment, said at a press conference that afternoon. Civil servants and public employees would take the five statutory Tet days, two before the new year and three after, covering Feb. 4 through Feb. 8. Feb. 6 and 7 fall on a Saturday and Sunday, so they would receive compensatory days on Feb. 9 and 10. The break would span the 28th day of the last lunar month of the Year of the Horse through the fifth day of the first lunar month of the Year of the Goat. Staff would return to work on the sixth day of Tet , Feb. 11. A seven-day break would give people working far from home more time to prepare and travel for the holiday, Quyen said. Private employers would set their own Tet schedules for workers based on the civil service calendar. The ministry circulated two options to ministries and agencies in early August. The other ran 10 days. For National Day in 2027, the ministry has proposed a four-day break from Sept. 2 to Sept. 5, combining the two statutory days, Sept. 2 and 3, with the weekend. Vietnam has 12 paid public holidays a year: one for New Year's Day, five for Tet , one for the Hung Kings Commemoration, one for Reunification Day on April 30, one for International Labor Day on May 1, and two for National Day. The 12th is Vietnam Culture Day on Nov. 24, which a National Assembly resolution added this year.

picked.t: PM urges Indian groups to invest in clean energy, infrastructure in Vietnam
picked.body: The Government leader made the suggestions on Saturday while meeting with ACME Vice Chairman Sanjay Dhawan and founder and Chairman Grandhi Mallikarjuna Rao of GMR Group in New Delhi on the occasion of his attendance at the 18th BRICS Summit and bilateral engagements in India. ACME, which specializes in clean energy and sustainable development, has developed renewable energy projects totaling more than 8GW in capacity across India. In Vietnam, the group has yet to make a large-scale direct investment but has signed an agreement in principle with a Vietnamese enterprise on long-term supply of materials for green steel production. Sanjay said ACME wishes to promote strategic cooperation with Vietnam in supplying and developing raw material value chains. The group is also interested in exploring investment opportunities, technology transfer, trade cooperation; and developing clean energy projects in Vietnam, he added. PM Hung affirmed that Vietnam welcomes major Indian corporations with strong technological capabilities to step up investment in Vietnam, particularly in areas where India has strengths and Vietnam has demand, such as clean energy, green industry, new materials, high technology, infrastructure, and digital transformation, in line with Vietnam’s investment attraction orientations in the coming time. He said Vietnam is implementing national strategies and plans for green transition, identifying renewable energy, new energy, green hydrogen, energy storage technology, and emissions reduction solutions as priority areas. With its experience and capabilities, ACME has considerable room to expand cooperation in Vietnam, he noted. Recognizing ACME’s orientation to develop an integrated value chain spanning renewable energy and green hydrogen to low-emission materials and industrial decarbonisation, the Vietnamese leader welcomed stronger connections and cooperation between the group and Vietnamese businesses in emissions-reduction solutions. He said Vietnam is preparing to amend its Investment Law toward shifting from broad-based investment attraction towards selective investment, prioritizing projects using advanced technologies, promoting innovation, generating added value, participating in global value chains and contributing to green transition. He suggested ACME study expanded cooperation and investment in Vietnam through large-scale projects that create added value and connect with regional markets. Such projects, he said, could help Vietnam become not only a market for green products but also an investment destination, production base and link in regional value chains meeting international standards. He also urged the firm to consider green and renewable-energy projects in Vietnam, while increasing technology transfer, human-resource training, business connectivity and ecosystem development to help establish green industrial value chains. The Vietnamese Government will create favorable conditions for businesses with strong capabilities, technologies and long-term visions to expand cooperation and investment in the country, the PM said, expressing his hope that ACME will become one of the pioneering Indian enterprises implementing exemplary projects that apply new technologies, making practical contributions to Vietnam-India trade and investment ties.The same day, PM Hung met with founder and Chairman Grandhi Mallikarjuna Rao and several executives of GMR Group, one of India’s leading infrastructure conglomerates. Rao gave an overview of GMR's operations in airport development and operation, energy, transport and urban infrastructure, saying that the group is interested in exploring cooperation and investment opportunities in Vietnam, particularly in airport and aviation infrastructure. He said that in May 2026, GMR signed memoranda of understanding with several Vietnamese businesses to study potential cooperation in airport development and operation, consulting services, airport technology and related areas. He expressed the group's wish to further expand cooperation and contribute to the development of Vietnam's aviation infrastructure. PM Hung affirmed that Vietnam always attaches importance to its relations with India, stressing that the Enhanced Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, underpinned by political trust and substantial untapped cooperation potential, provides favorable conditions for businesses of the two countries to expand cooperation in economy, trade, investment, science and technology, and infrastructure connectivity. He spoke highly of group's experience in developing and operating aviation infrastructure, noting that Vietnam identifies aviation infrastructure development as a priority to strengthen international connectivity, promote trade and tourism, and attract investment. Vietnam plans to develop a network of 36 airports by 2030 and continue expanding it towards 2050, he added. picked.t: Keppel expands digital learning initiative to over 2,300 Hanoi students
picked.body: Keppel, in collaboration with Tien Phong newspaper, with the support from ADG National Investment and Technology Development Corporation has expanded its "Bytes for Future" initiative to Hanoi, providing 55 computers, 90 headsets and two smart TVs to Son Dong Primary School – Song Phuong Branch and Van Canh Primary & Secondary School – Van Canh Secondary School Branch in Son Dong Commune. The expansion marks the initiative's first deployment in Hanoi and brings the total number of students reached across Vietnam to more than 4,400 since its launch in 2024. The schools previously had limited access to digital equipment, with two to four students sometimes sharing a computer and some existing devices outdated. The new equipment is expected to improve students' access to digital resources and help teachers incorporate more technology into lessons. Launch ceremonies were held at both schools on Sept. 11, attended by Nguyen Duy Cuong, Deputy Chief of Office of the Hanoi National Assembly Delegation and People's Council and former Vice Chairman of the Son Dong Commune People's Committee, and Joseph Low, Chief Representative of Keppel in Vietnam and President of Vietnam Real Estate at Keppel. Joseph said digital skills are increasingly important as digitalization and artificial intelligence reshape industries. "Through 'Bytes for Future,' we hope to help students build the capabilities and confidence needed to participate in and benefit from an increasingly technology-driven economy," he said. "As Keppel continues to grow its presence in Vietnam, we are pleased to extend this initiative to Hanoi and support the local community. This reflects our commitment to creating meaningful and lasting positive impact in the communities where we operate." Nguyen Duy Cuong, Deputy Chief of Office of the Hanoi National Assembly Delegation and People's Council and former Vice Chairman of the Son Dong Commune People's Committee, believes that the "Bytes for Future" initiative will help students in Son Dong Commune overcome barriers to accessing technology and open up opportunities for them to access modern knowledge. "It'll also lay a strong foundation for the continued development of education in the local community." On Son Dong Primary School's side, Principal Nguyen Manh Hanh said that the timely support and care from Keppel and Tien Phong Newspaper through the initiative are truly meaningful. "The practical donation of computers, together with their encouragement and support, has helped address some of the challenges faced by our school and created better conditions for our teachers and students in teaching and learning, particularly in accessing information technology – an area that is increasingly important in today's digital age." Le Duc Thuan, Principal of Van Canh Primary and Secondary School, said: "We particularly appreciate the message behind the ‘Bytes for Future' initiative: by giving students computers, we are not simply providing equipment, but also giving them more opportunities to learn, explore and move forward in life."
